title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription service is alleged to have recorded work meetings without the knowledge or consent of all participants. According to the lawsuit, the system recorded by default when a meeting host with an Otter account had the service linked to their calendar, and participants were not alerted that their audio would be captured and sent to Otter for AI training purposes. The failure occurred at the point of deployment, where a system designed to transcribe meetings was enabled without adequate notification or affirmative consent from all parties being recorded.

The company relied on a checkbox in its privacy policy as evidence of permission, but the lawsuit challenges whether this constitutes meaningful consent when participants in a meeting may have no direct interaction with that policy. The suit alleges that anonymization of data before AI training does not address the core problem of non-consensual recording. It is not established whether Otter's practices violated applicable law, whether the default recording behavior was intentional, or whether participants could have opted out at the meeting level rather than the account level.

Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service, of secretly recording private work conversations without proper consent. The company's Otter Notebook tool, which transcribes Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams meetings, allegedly records discussions by default without alerting participants that their audio will be shared with Otter to improve its artificial intelligence systems. Plaintiff Justin Brewer claims his privacy was invaded when he discovered Otter had covertly recorded a confidential conversation. The suit argues this violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws. Otter currently serves approximately 25 million users who have recorded over 1 billion meetings since the company's founding in 2016.

The lawsuit challenges Otter's claims that it obtains permission through a checkbox in its privacy policy and that it anonymizes data before using it for AI training. The suit alleges that when a meeting host has an Otter account linked to their calendar, the software can join and record meetings without obtaining consent from participants. Previous complaints on social media platforms described instances where Otter recordings included sensitive business information and raised concerns about data sharing with third parties, though Otter states it does not share data with foreign governments. Neither Brewer's legal team nor Otter representatives responded to requests for comment.
